concepts.conceptName: What is Ruby on Rails and what is the MVC architecture?
concepts.meaning: Ruby on Rails is a server-side web application framework written in Ruby under the MIT License. It follows the Model-View-Controller architectural pattern, emphasizing Convention over Configuration and Don't Repeat Yourself principles.

questions.q: What is Ruby on Rails?
questions.a: Ruby on Rails (RoR) is a full-stack web framework built on the Ruby programming language. It provides default structures for a database, a web service, and web pages. It encourages rapid development by using design patterns like Convention over Configuration (CoC) and Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY), meaning developers write less boilerplate code.
p: Full-stack web framework built on Ruby
Follows Convention over Configuration (CoC)
Promotes the Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) principle
Accelerates web application development

questions.q: What is the MVC architecture?
questions.a: MVC stands for Model-View-Controller. It is a software design pattern that separates an application into three interconnected components. The Model manages data and business logic, the View handles the user interface and presentation, and the Controller acts as an intermediary that processes user requests, interacts with the Model, and selects the appropriate View.
p: Model: Manages data, database interactions, and business logic
View: Handles the user interface and renders data to the user
Controller: Processes user input and coordinates between Model and View
Separation of concerns makes code maintainable and testable

questions.q: What are the core OOPs principles in Ruby?
questions.a: Ruby is a purely object-oriented language. Its four core OOPs principles are Encapsulation (bundling data and methods together), Inheritance (sharing behavior between parent and child classes), Polymorphism (using a unified interface for different data types), and Abstraction (hiding complex implementation details and showing only essential features).
p: Encapsulation: Hides internal state using public/private scopes
Inheritance: Allows classes to inherit methods and attributes from parent classes
Polymorphism: Enables different classes to respond to the same method call
Abstraction: Exposes only relevant features while hiding complex logic

questions.q: What is the difference between symbols and strings in Ruby?
questions.a: Strings are mutable objects and represent human-readable text, meaning every time a string is defined, a new memory object is allocated. Symbols are immutable, lightweight, and unique identifiers prefixed with a colon (e.g., :symbol). Because they are immutable and have a single instance in memory, symbols are commonly used as hash keys and for internal identifiers to improve performance.
p: Strings are mutable and consume more memory
Symbols are immutable and globally unique (:symbol)
Symbols are faster for lookups and commonly used as hash keys
Use strings for text manipulation and symbols for identifiers

concepts.conceptName: What are the four main OOPs principles and how are they implemented in Ruby?
concepts.meaning: Object-Oriented Programming in Ruby revolves around four core principles: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction, which help organize code into reusable and maintainable structures.

questions.q: What are the four main OOPs principles?
questions.a: The four main OOPs principles are Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction. Encapsulation bundles data and methods within a class and controls access using public, private, and protected keywords. Inheritance allows a class to inherit behaviors from a parent class using the '<' symbol. Polymorphism enables different classes to respond to the same method call. Abstraction hides complex implementation details and exposes only necessary features through interfaces or modules.
p: Encapsulation: Bundling data and hiding internal state.
Inheritance: Reusing code via parent-child class relationships.
Polymorphism: Using a uniform interface for different types.
Abstraction: Hiding complexity and showing only essentials.

questions.q: What is the difference between private, protected, and public methods in Ruby?
questions.a: Public methods can be called by anyone; they form the public interface of the class. Protected methods can be invoked only by objects of the defining class or its subclasses. Private methods are strictly internal and can only be called implicitly on the current object; they cannot be called with an explicit receiver, not even on 'self'. In Ruby, methods defined below the 'private' or 'protected' keyword take on that visibility.
p: Public: Accessible from anywhere.
Protected: Accessible within the class hierarchy.
Private: Accessible only within the context of the current object without an explicit receiver.

questions.q: What are the basic data types in Ruby?
questions.a: Ruby is fully object-oriented, so everything is an object, including basic data types. Common data types include Numbers (Integer, Float), Strings, Booleans (TrueClass, FalseClass), Symbols, Arrays, and Hashes. Symbols are immutable, reusable identifiers often used as hash keys, while Strings are mutable sequences of characters.
p: Everything in Ruby is an object.
Numbers include both Integer and Float.
Symbols are immutable, lightweight identifiers (:symbol).
Collections include Arrays and Hashes.

questions.q: How do you handle exceptions in Ruby?
questions.a: Exceptions in Ruby are handled using the 'begin', 'rescue', 'ensure', and 'end' blocks. Code that might raise an error is placed inside the 'begin' block. If an error occurs, execution jumps to the 'rescue' block where the exception can be caught and handled. The 'ensure' block contains code that always executes regardless of whether an exception occurred or not, commonly used for cleanup tasks like closing database connections.
p: Use 'begin' to wrap risky code.
Use 'rescue' to catch and handle errors.
Use 'ensure' for guaranteed cleanup execution.
Raise custom errors using 'raise'.

p: Strings are mutable; Symbols are immutable.
Strings allocate new memory each time; Symbols are reused (singleton objects).
Symbols are faster for comparisons and commonly used as hash keys.

questions.q: What are the four main Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) principles in Ruby?

Inheritance allows a class to inherit behaviors from a parent class. Polymorphism lets different classes respond to the same method interface. Abstraction hides complex implementation details and exposes only the essential features.
p: Encapsulation: Bundling data and restricting access.
Inheritance: Reusing code through parent-child class relationships.
Polymorphism: Different objects responding to the same method call.
Abstraction: Hiding internal complexity.

questions.q: Explain the difference between 'nil', 'false', and 'truthy' in Ruby.
questions.a: In Ruby, everything evaluates to true in a conditional statement except 'false' and 'nil'. 'false' is an instance of FalseClass, and 'nil' is an instance of NilClass, representing the absolute absence of a value. Both 'false' and 'nil' are considered 'falsy'. Any other object, including integers, empty strings, and arrays, is considered 'truthy' because only 'false' and 'nil' evaluate to false in conditionals.
p: Only 'false' and 'nil' are falsy in Ruby.
Everything else (including 0, '', and []) is truthy.
'nil' represents the absence of a value; 'false' represents a boolean failure.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'self' and 'super' keywords in Ruby?
questions.a: 'self' refers to the current object context, allowing methods to call other methods on the same object or reference the current class/instance. 'super' is used within subclass methods to call the method with the same name in the parent (superclass). It automatically passes the current arguments to the parent method unless called as 'super()' with no arguments.
p: 'self' points to the current object or class context.
'super' invokes the parent class's method of the same name.
Used extensively in class inheritance and method overriding.

questions.q: How do you handle exceptions in Ruby using rescue?
questions.a: You handle exceptions in Ruby by wrapping risky code inside a 'begin' and 'end' block, and using the 'rescue' keyword to catch and handle specific errors. You can capture the error object into a variable using '=> e'. Additionally, Ruby provides an 'ensure' block that executes code regardless of whether an exception occurred, which is ideal for cleanup tasks like closing database connections.
p: Use 'begin' and 'end' blocks around error-prone code.
Use 'rescue' to catch exceptions and prevent application crashes.
Use 'ensure' for cleanup logic that must always run.

concepts.conceptName: What is the difference between nil, false, and truthy values in Ruby?
concepts.meaning: Understanding Ruby's conditional evaluation rules, specifically how nil and false represent falsy states while everything else is truthy.

questions.q: What is the difference between nil and false in Ruby?
questions.a: In Ruby, 'false' is an instance of FalseClass and represents a boolean boolean value. On the other hand, 'nil' is an instance of NilClass and represents the absence of a value or a null reference. Both evaluate to falsy in conditional statements, but they are distinct objects with different methods and purposes.
p: false is an instance of FalseClass.
nil is an instance of NilClass (absence of value).
Both evaluate to falsy in conditional statements.

questions.q: What is a truthy value in Ruby?
questions.a: A truthy value is any value that evaluates to true in a boolean context, such as an if statement. In Ruby, only 'nil' and 'false' are falsy. Every other object—including integers (even 0), empty strings (''), and empty arrays ([])—is considered strictly truthy.
p: Everything except nil and false is truthy.
0 and empty strings are truthy in Ruby.
Truthy values evaluate to true in conditionals.

questions.q: How does Ruby treat 0 and empty strings in conditional statements?
questions.a: Unlike some other languages like JavaScript or Python, Ruby treats both the number 0 and empty strings ('') as truthy values. Only 'false' and 'nil' are treated as falsy. Therefore, an 'if 0' or 'if ""' statement will always execute its block.
p: 0 is truthy in Ruby.
Empty strings ('') are truthy in Ruby.
Only nil and false trigger falsy conditions.

concepts.conceptName: What are attr_reader, attr_writer, and attr_accessor?
concepts.meaning: Ruby shorthand methods used to automatically generate getter and setter methods for instance variables, controlling access to class attributes.

questions.q: What is attr_reader and when do you use it?
questions.a: attr_reader is a Ruby method that automatically generates a getter method for an instance variable, allowing it to be read (accessed) from outside the class. You use it when you want an attribute to be publicly viewable but protected from external modification, enforcing read-only access for data encapsulation.
p: Generates only the getter method.
Allows reading the instance variable.
Does not allow modifying the value.
Enforces read-only encapsulation.

questions.q: What is the difference between attr_writer and attr_reader?
questions.a: The primary difference lies in the direction of data access. attr_reader only generates a getter method to read an instance variable, whereas attr_writer only generates a setter method to assign or modify the value of an instance variable from outside the class. Neither method provides both capabilities simultaneously.
p: attr_reader = Read-only access.
attr_writer = Write-only access.
attr_reader creates a getter method.
attr_writer creates a setter method.

questions.q: What is attr_accessor and how does it relate to attr_reader and attr_writer?
questions.a: attr_accessor is a convenient shortcut in Ruby that combines both attr_reader and attr_writer. Instead of writing separate methods for getting and setting an instance variable, attr_accessor automatically generates both the getter and setter methods for you, allowing full read and write access to the attribute.
p: Combines reader and writer functionality.
Generates both getter and setter methods.
Allows full read and write access.
Reduces boilerplate code in classes.

questions.q: Why do we use attr_* methods instead of directly accessing instance variables in Ruby?
questions.a: Directly accessing instance variables from outside a class violates encapsulation principles in Object-Oriented Programming. Ruby does not expose instance variables publicly by default. Using attr_reader, attr_writer, or attr_accessor provides a clean, controlled interface to interact with your object's data while maintaining proper encapsulation.
p: Enforces OOP encapsulation principles.
Prevents direct unsafe variable access.
Provides a clean public interface.
Avoids writing manual getter/setter methods.

concepts.conceptName: What is the difference between local, instance, class, and global variables in Ruby?
concepts.meaning: Understanding variable scopes in Ruby is fundamental for managing state and data visibility across methods, objects, and the entire application.

questions.q: What is the difference between local, instance, class, and global variables in Ruby?
questions.a: Variables in Ruby are distinguished by their prefix symbols. Local variables (lowercase or underscore) are restricted to a single block or method. Instance variables (@ prefix) belong to a specific object instance. Class variables (@@ prefix) are shared across a class and its subclasses. Global variables ($ prefix) are accessible from anywhere in the entire Ruby program, though they are generally discouraged due to maintenance issues.
p: Local: No prefix, local scope to a method or block.
Instance: Starts with @, belongs to a specific object instance.
Class: Starts with @@, shared across the class and its descendants.
Global: Starts with $, accessible application-wide.

p: Encapsulation: Bundling data and hiding internal state.
Abstraction: Hiding complex implementation details.
Inheritance: Reusing code through parent-child class relationships.

questions.q: What is the difference between String#freeze and immutability in Ruby?
questions.a: In Ruby, strings are mutable by default. Calling the 'freeze' method on a string prevents any further modifications to that specific object, raising a RuntimeError if modified. However, freeze is a shallow immutability mechanism. To create a completely frozen string automatically upon creation, you can use the frozen_string_literal: true magic comment at the top of a Ruby file.
p: Mutable by default: Ruby strings can be changed in place.
freeze method: Locks a specific string object against modifications.
frozen_string_literal: Magic comment to freeze all string literals in a file.

questions.q: What are the basic built-in data types in Ruby?
questions.a: Ruby is fully object-oriented, meaning everything is an object, including primitive data types. Common built-in data types include numbers (Integer, Float), text (String, Symbol), collections (Array, Hash), booleans (TrueClass, FalseClass), and ranges (Range). Unlike some other languages, Ruby does not have primitive types; even numbers and booleans are instances of classes.
p: Numbers: Integer and Float.
Text: String and Symbol (immutable identifiers).
Collections: Array (ordered list) and Hash (key-value store).
Booleans: true and false (instances of TrueClass and FalseClass).

concepts.conceptName: What are ActiveRecord validations and what are some common validation helpers?
concepts.meaning: ActiveRecord validations are rules defined in Rails models to ensure only valid data is saved to the database, protecting data integrity by checking attributes before hitting SQL operations.

questions.q: What are ActiveRecord validations?
questions.a: ActiveRecord validations are methods used to ensure that only valid data is saved into your database. They are evaluated before saving an object (such as create or update), and if any validation fails, the save operation is aborted and error messages are added to the object's errors collection.
p: Run before database persistence
Protect database data integrity
Add errors to object when failing

questions.q: What are some common validation helpers in Rails?
questions.a: Common validation helpers include 'presence' (ensures an attribute is not blank), 'uniqueness' (ensures the value is unique in the table), 'length' (validates attribute character length), 'numericality' (ensures the value is numeric), and 'format' (checks values against a regular expression).
p: presence: checks for non-blank values
uniqueness: ensures no duplicate entries
length: restricts character count
numericality: enforces numbers only

questions.q: How do you check if an ActiveRecord object is valid and how do you view errors?
questions.a: You can check if an object is valid by calling the instance method .valid?, which returns true or false. If it returns false, you can inspect the specific validation errors by calling .errors or .errors.full_messages to get a human-readable array of error descriptions.
p: Use .valid? to check status
Use .errors to access error details
Use .errors.full_messages for strings

questions.q: What is the difference between create, save, and their bang (!) counterparts regarding validations?
questions.a: Non-bang methods like save and create run validations automatically and return false if the validation fails, without raising an exception. Bang methods like save! and create! also run validations, but if they fail, they raise an ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid exception, halting execution.
p: save/create return false on failure
save!/create! raise exceptions on failure
Both trigger model validations

questions.q: What is the difference between render and redirect_to in Rails controllers?
questions.a: The 'render' method processes the template and sends the response back to the browser within the same request lifecycle, preserving instance variables. In contrast, 'redirect_to' tells the browser to issue a completely new HTTP request to a different URL, clearing instance variables and requiring new data loading.

redirect_to triggers a new HTTP request and resets variables
render is faster; redirect_to involves an extra round-trip

concepts.conceptName: How do database migrations work in Ruby on Rails?
concepts.meaning: Database migrations are a Ruby DSL-based feature in Rails that allows developers to evolve the database schema consistently and persistently over time across different environments.

questions.q: What is a database migration in Ruby on Rails?
questions.a: A migration is a Ruby class that allows you to define changes to your database schema in a structured, database-independent way. Instead of writing raw SQL, you use Rails methods like create_table or add_column. This allows your team to share database changes easily and run them across different environments like development, test, and production.
p: Ruby-based DSL for database changes
Database-independent schema evolution
Tracks execution using the schema_migrations table

questions.q: What is the difference between `change`, `up`, and `down` methods in migrations?
questions.a: The `change` method is the primary way to write migrations. Rails knows how to reverse these migrations automatically (e.g., `add_column` can be undone with `remove_column`). The `up` and `down` methods are used for reversible migrations that are too complex for Rails to figure out automatically. `up` describes what the migration does, and `down` describes how to revert it.
p: change: automatically reversible by Rails
up: defines forward database changes
down: defines rollback instructions for complex changes

questions.q: How do you roll back a database migration in Rails?
questions.a: You roll back the most recent migration by running the terminal command `rails db:rollback`. You can also roll back multiple steps by appending the STEP argument, such as `rails db:rollback STEP=3`, which reverts the last three applied migrations by executing their corresponding `down` methods or reversing their `change` methods.
p: Command: rails db:rollback
Reverts the most recent migration
Can specify steps using STEP=n

questions.q: What is the purpose of the `db/schema.rb` file?
questions.a: The `db/schema.rb` file is generated and updated by Rails after every migration. It represents the current state of your database schema. Instead of running every migration from scratch—which can take a long time for mature apps—Rails uses `db:schema:load` to quickly set up a new database directly from this file.
p: Represents the current database state
Auto-generated after running migrations
Used for fast database setup via db:schema:load

concepts.conceptName: What are the different types of ActiveRecord associations in Rails?
concepts.meaning: ActiveRecord associations create a connection between two Active Record models, making common operations simpler and more efficient by defining relationships like belongs_to, has_one, has_many, and has_and_belongs_to_many.

questions.q: What are the different types of ActiveRecord associations in Rails?
questions.a: Rails supports six main types of associations: belongs_to, has_one, has_many, has_many :through, has_one :through, and has_and_belongs_to_many. These associations link models together, allowing Rails to automatically generate SQL queries to fetch related data, manage foreign keys, and handle data integrity effortlessly during record creation, updates, and deletion.
p: belongs_to and has_one handle singular 1-to-1 connections.
has_many handles 1-to-many connections.
has_many :through and has_and_belongs_to_many handle many-to-many connections.

questions.q: Explain the difference between belongs_to and has_one.
questions.a: Both represent a one-to-one association, but they differ in where the foreign key is placed. The model with the 'belongs_to' association holds the foreign key column in its database table. The 'has_one' model indicates that another model points to it. For example, a User 'has_one' Profile, and the Profiles table contains the user_id foreign key, meaning Profile 'belongs_to' User.
p: belongs_to holds the foreign key in its table.
has_one does not hold the foreign key.
Used together to establish a 1-to-1 relationship.

questions.q: What is the difference between has_many and has_and_belongs_to_many?
questions.a: A 'has_many' association is typically used in a one-to-many relationship, or in a many-to-many relationship when using 'has_many :through' with a join model. A 'has_and_belongs_to_many' (HABTM) association creates a direct many-to-many connection using an un-modeled join table without a primary key. HABTM is simpler for basic many-to-many links, while has_many :through is preferred when you need validations or extra attributes on the join table.
p: has_many can represent one-to-many or many-to-many via :through.

questions.q: What is a polymorphic association in Rails?
questions.a: A polymorphic association allows a model to belong to more than one other model on a single association. For example, a Picture model might belong to either an Employee or a Product. Instead of having separate employee_id and product_id foreign keys, the table uses an imageable_id and an imageable_type string column to store the parent model's class name and ID.
p: Enables a model to belong to multiple models through a single association.
Uses two columns: _id and _type.
Reduces database redundancy for shared resources like comments or attachments.

questions.a: The `begin` block wraps code that might raise an error. If an exception occurs, execution jumps to the `rescue` block to handle it safely. questions.q: How do you manually trigger an exception using the raise keyword?

questions.q: What is the base class for all standard exceptions in Ruby?
questions.a: The base class for all standard, catchable exceptions in Ruby is `StandardError`. When you use `rescue` without specifying an error class, it rescues `StandardError` and its descendants. It is considered a best practice to rescue `StandardError` rather than the root `Exception` class, which also covers system exits and syntax errors.

Avoid rescuing the root Exception class
Inherits from Exception

questions.q: What is the difference between preload, eager_load, and includes in Active Record, and when should you use each?
questions.a: preload always loads associated records using separate queries. eager_load forces a single query using a LEFT OUTER JOIN. includes acts as a dynamic wrapper: it defaults to preload (separate queries) unless conditions reference the associated table via where or order, in which case it behaves like eager_load. Explicitly using preload or eager_load is preferred in complex queries to prevent unintended query plans, memory bloat from cartesian products, or ambiguous column errors.

eager_load executes a single query with LEFT OUTER JOIN

questions.q: How do polymorphic associations work under the hood, and what database indexing strategy is required?
questions.a: Polymorphic associations allow a single model to belong to multiple parent models using two columns: an integer/UUID ID column ([name]_id) and a string type column ([name]_type). Active Record uses the type column to instantiate the correct Ruby class. For performance, a composite index must be created on both columns (e.g., add_index :comments, [:commentable_type, :commentable_id]). Without this composite index, queries looking up polymorphic children cause full table scans.

Determines Ruby class dynamically at runtime
Requires a composite index on [:type, :id]
Prevents full table scans on associated lookups

questions.q: How does ActiveRecord::Relation#merge work, and why is it preferred over raw joins conditions?

questions.a: `preload` always executes two separate queries, minimizing database complexity and avoiding Cartesian products, but requires loading IDs into Ruby memory. `eager_load` executes a single LEFT OUTER JOIN, pushing filtering to the database but risking massive memory footprints via Cartesian explosions on 1:N:M relations. `includes` dynamically chooses between them, but heuristic guessing can sub-optimally optimize complex queries under high production load.

includes: Heuristic-based wrapper; unpredictable in complex dependency trees.

Raw SQL minimizes memory by avoiding ActiveRecord model instantiation, mapping directly to POROs or hashes, and allows leveraging advanced database-specific query planner hints.

concepts.conceptName: Global VM Lock (GVL) Interplay with Multi-threading and Evented I/O
concepts.meaning: Advanced analysis of how MRI's Global VM Lock governs thread concurrency, C-extension yielding, and its architectural friction with event-driven I/O models in high-throughput Ruby on Rails environments.

questions.q: How does MRI Ruby's GVL implementation impact thread scheduling when mixing CPU-bound tasks and blocking C-extensions?
questions.a: The GVL ensures only one thread executes Ruby bytecode at a time, preventing true CPU parallelism. However, C-extensions (like native database drivers) can explicitly release the GVL using `rb_thread_call_without_gvl`, allowing other Ruby threads to run concurrently. Without this explicit release, blocking C calls starve the entire Ruby thread pool, crippling throughput.

C-extensions can bypass the GVL to achieve native concurrency.
Blocking calls without GVL release cause massive thread starvation.

questions.q: In a Puma multi-threaded Rails setup, why doesn't increasing the thread count indefinitely scale performance for I/O-bound applications?
questions.a: While I/O operations release the GVL allowing other threads to run, thread context switching overhead, OS scheduler limits, and memory consumption per thread eventually plateau throughput. Furthermore, if the database connection pool is smaller than the thread count, threads spend excessive time waiting for connections, leading to lock contention rather than genuine concurrency gains.
p: I/O operations temporarily release the GVL.
Excessive threads cause OS context-switch overhead.
Database connection pool limits negate high thread counts.

questions.q: How do evented I/O servers like Async or Falcon interact with the GVL compared to traditional thread-per-request servers like Puma?
questions.a: Evented architectures utilize non-blocking fibers and event loops (like epoll/kqueue). When a fiber awaits I/O, it yields control back to the event loop without blocking the underlying OS thread. While the GVL still restricts execution to one fiber at a time on that thread, cooperative scheduling avoids OS-level thread switching overhead and maximizes resource utilization.
p: Evented servers use non-blocking fibers instead of OS threads.
Fibers yield control cooperatively during I/O.
Reduces OS context-switching overhead under heavy load.

questions.q: Diagnose a production scenario where a Rails app experiences latency spikes under load despite low CPU utilization. How is the GVL involved?

Threads might be waiting on a congested resource (e.g., synchronous external API, saturated DB pool) while holding the GVL or blocking thread scheduling ticks. Profiling with rbspy or Stackprof is required to identify C-extensions or native calls failing to release the GVL.

Threads may hold the GVL while waiting on external resources.

questions.q: How does ActiveRecord ensure thread safety when checking out connections from the ConnectionPool in a multi-threaded server like Puma?
questions.a: ActiveRecord uses a ReentrantMutex (`Monitor`) inside `ConnectionPool` to synchronize access to the connection queue. When a thread requests a connection via `connection_pool.with_connection`, it acquires the monitor lock, checks out an available connection tied to the current thread's Thread-Local Storage (TLS), and releases the lock. If exhausted, it waits up to `checkout_timeout` seconds, guarded by a condition variable, before raising a `ConnectionTimeoutError`.

Connections map to Thread-Local Storage.
Condition variables handle timeout waits.

questions.q: What exact memory and performance degradation occurs in MRI Ruby when the ActiveRecord connection pool becomes fully saturated?

In MRI, while threads wait on the Monitor mutex, they don't release the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) efficiently for IO in all ActiveRecord layers, causing thread starvation. Memory footprint spikes due to queued request objects, and garbage collection pressure increases from short-lived synchronization objects created during timeout waits.

Request queuing spikes memory footprint.
Timeout waits increase GC pressure.

If Sidekiq worker threads (running on the same or separate processes sharing a pool) attempt to execute immediately and demand connections, the pool saturates. Web threads block waiting for background jobs or subsequent queries, while background threads starve, creating a circular wait condition that freezes the application.

Shared pools cause resource starvation.

Inside an around_save block, executing queries without explicit reloading or misuse of association caching frequently triggers hidden N+1 queries because database interactions inside the yield lack batching context, bypassing bulk insert/update optimizations.
